@graph.name: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP)

provenance.section_title: Critical Question 2: Summary and Future Research; Critical Question 3: Parenteral Antibiotics in ED

rules.rationale: Adult patients diagnosed with CAP in the ED may require parenteral antibiotics initially, potentially followed by oral treatment.
rules.citation: Appropriately selected antibiotics are the standard treatment for CAP, with outpatients generally treated orally and those requiring admission generally initially treated parenterally.

@graph.name: Patient clinically stable

provenance.section_title: Critical Question 2: Summary and Future Research; Critical Question 3: Parenteral Antibiotics in ED

rules.rationale: Clinical stability is a criterion for transitioning from parenteral to oral antibiotics.
rules.citation: These studies used various criteria to define when the parenteral to oral therapy switch should occur, but most mandate the patient be clinically stable and afebrile for a minimum of 24 to 72 hours.

rules.rationale: Afebrile status is a criterion for transitioning from parenteral to oral antibiotics.
rules.citation: These studies used various criteria to define when the parenteral to oral therapy switch should occur, but most mandate the patient be clinically stable and afebrile for a minimum of 24 to 72 hours.

@graph.name: Clinically stable and afebrile for a minimum of 24 to 72 hours

provenance.section_title: Critical Question 2: Summary and Future Research; Critical Question 3: Parenteral Antibiotics in ED

rules.rationale: Clinical stability and afebrile status for 24-72 hours are criteria used to determine when a patient can transition from parenteral to oral antibiotics in CAP.
rules.citation: With appropriate application of clinical decision aids, an increasing proportion of patients may be treated as outpatients or with periods of observation (<24 hours). In those patients requiring observation or for whom a brief admission or discharge is deemed to be a reasonable option (borderline cases), it would be reasonable to consider an initial parenteral dose of antibiotics prior to conversion to oral therapy. Our systematic review of the literature, however, found lack of evidence that assessed whether a single dose of parenteral antibiotics in the ED followed by oral treatment was safe or associated with improved outcomes when compared with oral treatment alone among patients either being admitted or discharged home.
